characteristics.roast: None — steam fixation instead of pan-firing

description.short: Rare needle-shaped green tea fixed with steam — an ancient Chinese technique largely superseded by pan-firing, sharing affinities with Japanese green tea
description.overview: One of China's few remaining steamed green teas. Steaming was the dominant processing method during the Tang and Song dynasties before pan-firing took over in the Ming dynasty (16th century).
description.leaf: Slender, straight, needle-like deep pine-green leaves with a vibrant glossy sheen
description.liquor: Vivid emerald green, crystal clear (steam fixation preserves chlorophyll exceptionally well)
description.aroma: Fresh, marine-vegetal, lightly savory with subtle nori seaweed notes reminiscent of Japanese sencha
description.taste: Vibrant, brisk, and savory with pronounced umami richness and natural sweetness
description.processing: Plucking tender shoots → steam fixation (zhenqing, rather than dry pan-firing) → rolling and straightening into fine needles on heated tables → drying

history.origin: Steam fixation was the standard method for green tea throughout Tang and Song dynasty China before being largely supplanted by dry wok pan-firing during the Ming dynasty
history.development: Enshi preserved this ancient method through centuries of relative geographical isolation, serving as a living museum of ancient Chinese tea craft
history.modern: While steaming became the hallmark of Japanese green tea production, in China it is extraordinarily rare outside of Enshi, making this tea a critical cultural treasure
interestingFacts: Because of the shared steam-fixation method, Enshi Yulu's brisk umami profile closely parallels premium Japanese sencha — a rare convergence of Chinese and Japanese tea craftsmanship
The traditional crafting technique of Enshi Yulu has been inscribed as a Chinese National Intangible Cultural Heritage
